reasoning: This is a narrative review article synthesizing existing literature on schizophrenia pathophysiology, cognition, and treatment. It does not report generation or use of any specific research software, nor does it generate or analyze any new research dataset. No computational tools or datasets are described as part of the methodology.

This is a clinical consensus guideline based on literature review and expert opinion. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it create or use a substantive research dataset; it synthesizes existing published evidence into recommendations.

The study uses existing research software (TopoToolbox V2) to analyze a nationwide DEM, which is a utility tool rather than newly created software. However, the research generates a new national-scale geodatabase of catchment and stream network characteristics for 128 catchments in the Philippines, creating substantive new research data (morphometric/topographic dataset) that did not exist before and is made accessible via a web application. This constitutes generated data (D1) alongside used software (S2).

The paper develops a new visualization tool/software integrating Jaya algorithm with Latin Hypercube Sampling for graph drawing, which is a novel software contribution created during the research (S1). It also generates synthetic datasets using the Erdős–Rényi model with varying nodes/edges for benchmarking, in addition to using some real-world datasets, constituting generated research data used to produce new findings about algorithm performance (D1).

This is a study protocol for a planned randomised clinical trial. No data has been collected or analyzed yet (it describes planned assessments), and no research software is created or used in generating findings. As per the rules, planned/proposed artefacts and protocols without actual data/software use should be classified as S3D3.

The study generated new survey/interview data from nurses and midwives (four cohorts, n=153) over 2019-22, along with qualitative thematic analysis from interviews, representing newly collected research data. There is no indication of software being developed or used in a substantive research sense—statistical analysis of survey data was likely done with standard tools (e.g., spreadsheet/statistics software) in a routine, non-research-generating capacity. Thus the paper fits No Research Software, Data Generated.

The abstract provides minimal information (title only, no abstract text) and appears to be an editorial/introduction to a special issue covering feature-driven ML and DL applications in finance, education, and healthcare. There is no evidence of specific software or data being generated or used within this paper itself—it seems to be a summary/overview article rather than an original research paper with concrete artifacts. Without clear evidence of software or data generation/use, it defaults to S3D3.

The study uses existing software/tools (TCP modeling, treatment planning systems for SIB dose escalation) rather than developing new software, so it falls under S2. However, the research generates new patient-specific data: ADC-derived cellular density maps, TCP maps, and biological target volumes (BTV) from DW-MRI scans of ten GBM patients - this is newly created research data specific to this study, not reuse of existing external datasets. Thus it is classified as D1 (Data Generated).

This is a translational pathology study generating new research data via multiplexed immunofluorescence on patient tissue samples (NLPHL and THRLBCL cases), quantifying immune cell phenotypes across histological patterns. This represents newly generated research data (D1). The multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging and quantification likely used existing image analysis software/platforms (e.g., imaging analysis tools for multiplex IF) as a utility to process and analyse the data, rather than creating new software - these tools generate new knowledge when applied to the novel dataset, so it is classified as software used (S2) rather than software generated or no software.

The study collected new survey data from 384 startup directors/representatives using BRCS, MBI-GS, and custom stress questionnaires, generating a novel dataset for burnout prediction (D1). For analysis, the researchers employed a GMDH neural network—an existing modeling technique/method rather than a newly created software tool—to analyze the data and extract effective parameters, which constitutes use of existing research software/method to generate new knowledge (S2). There is no indication that the authors developed or substantially extended a new software tool; they applied the established GMDH approach to their data.

The study reports a new crystal structure of Mcl-1 bound to AMG-176 and NMR-based conformer analysis of clinical inhibitors - generating new experimental research data (X-ray crystallography structures, NMR data) that produce novel knowledge about ligand prestructuring and induced fit. While standard crystallography/NMR processing software was likely used (e.g., data processing, refinement programs), these are utility tools not themselves generating new knowledge as research software outputs; no new software is described as created. Hence data is generated (D1) while software is only used as routine utility, falling under S3.

This is a cluster RCT generating new primary data (maternal/child outcome assessments at 5 time points across 8 clinics) specifically for this study, qualifying as D1. There is no mention of developing or using specialized research software for analysis beyond standard statistical tools used as utilities, so it falls under S3 (no research software).

The researchers developed new harmonised symptom/test phenotypes (coding definitions, not software) and derived novel data (classifications of symptom consultations) from linked EHR datasets (UK Biobank and CPRD linked to cancer registry), creating new substantive research data (phenotype-derived symptom rates) not previously existing. No mention of creating or substantially extending software tools; statistical analysis (Poisson models) was likely done with standard statistical packages used as utilities, not a research software contribution. Thus data is generated (D1) while software is not a focus (S3)."

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum. It does not report any empirical research involving software development/use or data collection/analysis; it is a conceptual discussion and literature-based argument without research artefacts.

The paper compiles and presents a novel global dataset (DOCU-CLIM) of 621 documentary climate time series, including previously unpublished data, which is clearly research data generated/compiled for this study creating new knowledge about historical climate. There is no indication of new research software being developed; the analysis (proxy forward models, correlations) likely uses standard statistical tools/utilities rather than a novel research software contribution, so it falls under No Research Software (S3) and Data Generated (D1).

The study generated novel sediment-core metabarcoding biodiversity data spanning 100 years alongside chemical pollution and climate records, which is newly produced research data (D1). It also developed a conceptual/explainable AI network model framework (multimodal learning network) specifically created for this research to link biodiversity and abiotic data, constituting generated research software (S1) that produced new knowledge about ecosystem functional changes.

This is a state-of-the-art narrative review summarizing existing literature on BBB imaging methods across various diseases and settings. It does not generate or substantively use any specific research software, nor does it create or analyze a particular dataset. It synthesizes published findings and discusses future directions, without reporting new data generation or software development/use that produces new knowledge.

This is a cross-sectional survey study that generated new primary data (a survey of 10,007 respondents collecting knowledge, vaccine uptake, and willingness data) in Malang, Indonesia - this is novel research data collected specifically for this study (D1). Statistical analyses were performed using standard software (linear regression, logistic regression, GSEM), but these are existing statistical tools used as utilities for analysis rather than research software created or extended by the authors (S2, since it's used but not generated, though not primary driver - standard stats packages are typically classified as S2 or S3 utility use). Since the software (e.g., Stata/SPSS for regression and GSEM) is used to generate novel analytical results from the collected data, this is software used (S2) rather than no software, and data generated (D1) since the survey data is newly collected.

This is a review article discussing concepts and challenges in post-GWAS interpretation of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease genetics. It does not generate or use specific software or datasets itself; it summarizes existing literature, tools, and findings without conducting original data analysis or software development.

This is a narrative review article summarizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not report generation or use of any specific research software, nor does it generate or analyze new research data; it synthesizes findings from other studies conceptually.

The paper creates a novel counterfactual GAN architecture specifically designed to generate synthetic OCT images and longitudinal time series, which is a new research software contribution central to generating new knowledge about retinal aging. The underlying OCT imaging data is from the existing UK Biobank population study (an existing dataset), used but not newly generated by this research - the researchers analyze pre-existing retrospective OCT images rather than creating new primary data. Thus this is S1 (software generated) and D2 (data used).

The researchers used an existing pre-trained model (GPT-2) and existing NLP metrics/embedding methods as tools, rather than creating new research software (the accompanying Python tutorial is a utility/documentation, not novel research software). However, they generated new simulated data - FTD-like narratives produced by systematically perturbing GPT-2's parameters (stochasticity, memory span) - which constitutes newly generated research data used to test theoretical hypotheses about thought disorder. This generated simulated text corpus is central to producing the paper's novel findings, qualifying as Data Generated (D1), while the software (GPT-2, sentence encoders) was used as existing tools (S2).

This is a study protocol describing a planned future survey. No actual data collection or software development has occurred yet - the survey will be designed and disseminated using existing commercial tool (Qualtrics), which is a utility rather than research software. Since this describes planned/proposed activities rather than completed research with actual artifacts used or generated, it falls under S3D3 per the general rules for protocol papers.

This is a clinical pharmacology study (phase 1 crossover trials) that generated new experimental data (pharmacokinetic parameters like Cmax, AUC, drug-drug interaction profiles) from human subjects dosed with rezafungin and various probe drugs. This data is newly generated research data (D1). There is no mention of custom research software being developed or used beyond standard statistical/bioanalytical tools, which are incidental utilities rather than research software central to generating new knowledge, so it falls under S3 (no research software).

The paper uses existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary assessment) but derives a new adherence score variable (the operationalised 2018 WCRF/AICR score) for 158,415-314,616 participants, representing newly generated research data (a novel scoring variable/dataset) that did not exist before. No new research software is described; only application of scoring rules/calculations, which is a methodological/analytical process rather than development of a reusable software tool generating new knowledge, so this is classified as S3 (no research software). Since substantive new data (the derived score dataset) was generated, this falls under D1.

This is a literature review discussing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, and ocular imaging approaches. It does not report generation or use of any specific research software, nor does it generate or analyze a specific dataset - it synthesizes existing literature and discusses future potential applications (e.g., conjunctival microvasculature imaging) without presenting new data or software artifacts.

The study uses existing Google Trends data (a publicly available data source) across multiple countries, analyzed with Joinpoint regression software. The data was used, not newly generated by the researchers themselves (Google collects and provides it), so it falls under 'Data Used' rather than 'Data Generated'. Joinpoint regression is a standard statistical analysis tool/utility used for analysis, not a research software created or substantively extended by the authors, so it counts as No Research Software (S3).

This qualitative study generated new primary data through semi-structured interviews with 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers, which was then thematically analyzed to derive novel findings (seven themes) about COVID-19's effects on dental service delivery in Fiji. This constitutes substantive research data generation (D1). The analysis was done manually (manual thematic analysis) with no mention of specialized research software being created or used beyond basic tools, so it falls under S3 (No Research Software).

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes data from 76 articles and two national surveys to compute pooled prevalence estimates (stunting, thinness, overweight/obesity, micronutrient deficiencies). The meta-analysis generates new aggregated/synthesized research data (pooled prevalence statistics) that did not exist before, constituting D1 (substantive data generated through synthesis). No research software was created or used in a substantive knowledge-generating way; standard statistical/meta-analysis tools would be utility software only, so S3 applies.

The study generated new experimental data (HD-sEMG recordings decomposed into motor unit firing patterns) from 18 children (TD vs DCD), which is novel research data created specifically for this study and forms the basis for new findings about motor unit variability. This qualifies as D1 (data generated). For software, the researchers used existing decomposition algorithms/software to process the EMG signals into motor unit action potential trains, but there is no indication they developed new software tools themselves - they used existing analysis software as a means to generate their findings, which still constitutes substantive use enabling new knowledge extraction (S2), rather than creating new software.
